preview: Soham Rane shares his off-campus interview experience for the Google SWE Summer Intern role, detailing the application process, phone screen, interview rounds, and preparation tips.
content: Google SWE Intern | Interview experience Mode: Off-Campus Soham Rane | TY IT 2023-27 Application Google did not visit on-campus for internships in 2025 (unlike previous year), so I applied off-campus on careers.google.com in July when they posted the SWE Summer Intern 2026 opening. I also took a referral from a senior (LY, who interned at Google in Summer 2025). It’s preferred to take referrals from full-time employees, as those generally carry more weight. Call for Interview (Phone Screen) On 17th September, an hour before my MST exam, I received the first call from Google. They asked if I was available to talk for ~10 minutes or if they should call later. I said yes and continued with the call. (Note: Only say yes if you are in the right environment to talk., they’re happy to reschedule otherwise. This quick call is called the “phone screen” round.) They asked for my introduction, projects, tech stack, DSA experience, and number of problems solved on LeetCode/Codeforces, etc. At the end of the call, they said they were happy to proceed with me for interviews and asked about my availability. Since it was my MST week, I requested a slot in the following week. Later that day, I received the confirmation email for the scheduled interview. Interview Preparation I quickly contacted seniors and took guidance, advice, and mock interviews from them. Google’s interview process is very structured. Each round has a strict 45 minute limit. You get a problem/problems, and you have to walk through your thought process with the interviewer. You solve it in a shared Google Doc. DSA skills are essential, it’s not something you can build in just a week or two, so keep practicing consistently and you’ll see steady improvement. Important points I focused on: State your assumptions clearly and ask clarifying questions. This is very important, because interviewers often provide an incomplete or minimal version of the problem to test your communication skills. We may end up making incorrect assumptions and solve the wrong problem, and only realize it near the end of the interview. So make sure to state your assumptions so you can catch errors early. Write clean, readable, well-structured code with good variable names Dry run the solution. Think of corner cases, but choose simple ones so you don’t waste time. Communicate your thought process clearly. It’s okay to take a minute of silence to think, but not too long. If stuck, communicate where you’re stuck, interviewers often give subtle hints. Time management is very important. Keep checking the clock. Pay attention to your interviewer. They’re not against you. They want you to solve the problem. They may drop tiny hints, so make sure to catch them. Before the interviews, I did a few mocks with seniors and friends. It helped me identify strengths and weaknesses. First Round I gave Round 1 on 26th September. I was asked 1 problem with a couple of follow-ups. Took exactly 45 minutes to answer everything. I can’t discuss the exact problems for confidentiality reasons. Second Round I received the mail for Round 2 a few days later. I gave this round on 7th October and was asked 1 problem. Initially, I gave a solution but later realized it was wrong when I dry-ran it on a test case given by the interviewer. Then I came up with the correct approach and dry-ran that one too. By that time, 35 minutes had passed. The interviewer ended the round without any follow-ups. Results After a long wait, I received the results on 12th November and I was fortunate enough to be selected. Final Thoughts The overall process requires a good amount of fortune to go your way. Many things are out of your control. Focus only on what you can control, give your best, and don’t think too much about the outcome. No matter what happens, you’ll come out a better version of yourself.
